subject: anatomy
title: Spleen Topography: Peritoneal Ligaments, Relations, and Surgical Risks

steps.tx: The spleen is the largest lymphoid organ in the body, situated in the left hypochondrium between the gastric fundus and the diaphragm. It is completely invested by peritoneum and suspended by two primary peritoneal folds: the **gastrosplenic ligament** connecting it to the stomach, and the lienorenal ligament connecting it to the left kidney.
steps.say: The spleen is the largest lymphoid organ, nestled in the left hypochondrium. It is suspended by the gastrosplenic ligament to the stomach and the lienorenal ligament to the left kidney.

vis.alt: Anatomical schematic showing spleen, splenic hilum, and peritoneal ligaments
vis.caption: Anatomical relations of the spleen, splenic pedicle, and peritoneal ligaments. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: The contents of the splenic ligaments are surgically critical during splenectomy. The gastrosplenic ligament transmits the **short gastric vessels** and left gastroepiploic vessels, whereas the lienorenal (splenorenal) ligament transmits the splenic artery and vein alongside the delicate tail of the pancreas.
steps.say: Splenic ligament contents are crucial during splenectomy. The gastrosplenic ligament contains short gastric vessels, while the lienorenal ligament carries splenic vessels and the pancreatic tail.

left.title: Gastrosplenic Ligament
points: Connects splenic hilum to greater curvature
Contains short gastric arteries and veins
Divided to enter the lesser sac

right.title: Lienorenal Ligament
points: Connects splenic hilum to anterior left kidney
Contains splenic artery and splenic vein
Contains the tail of the pancreas
Pancreatic injury risks fistula during ligation

steps.tx: When ligating the splenic vascular pedicle at the hilum during emergency splenectomy, accidental injury to the **tail of the pancreas** is the most common iatrogenic complication. Laceration or ischemic necrosis of the pancreatic tail produces a persistent postoperative external pancreatic fistula or painful peripancreatic fluid collection.
steps.say: Inadvertent damage to the pancreatic tail is a major hazard of splenectomy. Lacerating the tail within the lienorenal ligament produces a troublesome postoperative pancreatic fistula.

steps.tx: The visceral surface of the spleen exhibits three distinct impressions corresponding to adjacent organs: a large anterior gastric impression for the stomach fundus, an inferior renal impression resting against the left kidney, and a medial colic impression cradling the **splenic flexure** of the colon.
steps.say: The visceral surface shows three impressions: a gastric impression for the fundus, a renal impression for the left kidney, and a colic impression for the splenic flexure.

steps.tx: The superior border of the spleen is sharp and features one or two characteristic notches, termed the **splenic notch**. These notches represent embryological remnants of the multiple lobules that fused during development, providing a crucial bedside sign allowing clinical differentiation of an enlarged spleen from an enlarged left kidney.
steps.say: The superior border features notches representing embryonic lobules. Palpating a notch on the anterior border differentiates an enlarged spleen from an enlarged left kidney.

left.title: Splenomegaly Characteristics
points: Enlarges downwards and medially toward right iliac fossa
Features sharp anterior border with palpable notch
Cannot get above the mass under costal margin
Dull to percussion; not bimanually ballotable

right.title: Enlarged Left Kidney
points: Rounded smooth contour without any notches
Can get fingers above the mass in lean patients
Resonant due to overlying colon; bimanually ballotable

steps.tx: Fracture of the left lower ribs (ribs nine, ten, and eleven) frequently lacerates the spleen, the most commonly injured visceral organ in blunt abdominal trauma. Extravasation of blood irritates the diaphragmatic parietal pleura, provoking referred pain to the left shoulder tip mediated by the phrenic nerve (C3-C5), designated **Kehr sign**.
steps.say: Fractures of lower left ribs frequently lacerate the spleen. Hemoperitoneum irritates the diaphragm, causing referred left shoulder pain mediated by the phrenic nerve, termed Kehr sign.

steps.tx: Up to ten to fifteen percent of individuals possess one or more **accessory spleens** (splenculi), formed by failure of embryonic splenic buds to fuse completely. Typically located at the splenic hilum, gastrosplenic ligament, or greater omentum, an unrecognized accessory spleen can hypertrophy and cause recurrence of immune thrombocytopenia after splenectomy.
steps.say: Accessory spleens occur in up to fifteen percent of people from incomplete lobular fusion. Found near the hilum or omentum, missed tissue can cause disease relapse after splenectomy.

rows: Incomplete fusion of dorsal mesogastrium buds
Must be sought and excised in ITP
Easily missed during emergency trauma surgery
Can mimic peritoneal metastasis on CT
Descent of testis pulls splenic tissue
Presents as scrotal mass alongside testis

steps.tx: Surgical acid reduction for refractory peptic ulcer disease historically utilized selective **highly selective vagotomy** (parietal cell vagotomy). By transecting only the gastric branches of the anterior and posterior nerves of Latarjet while preserving the terminal crow-foot branches to the pyloric antrum, acid secretion is reduced while preserving normal pyloric emptying.
steps.say: Highly selective vagotomy cuts only the acid-secreting branches of the nerves of Latarjet while sparing the crow's foot to the pylorus, preserving normal gastric emptying without drainage surgery.
